sections.COMMENTS:
This Source is a NW-dipping blind fault that slipped during the 14 September 2003, Mw 5.3 earthquake with reverse kinematics. The strike, dip and rake of the fault were chosen following the focal solution of this event as calculated by Piccinini et al. (2006). The main shock occurred at 20 km of depth, and the aftershocks followed a NE-SW alignment, being confined between 15 and 22 km of depth. The earthquake, besides being felt over a wide area, did not produce any damage and the fault remained purely blind due to its depth.
Piccinini et al. (2006) analysed the 2003 seismic sequence and, on the basis of the depth distribution of the hypocenters of the aftershocks, suggested that the main shock occurred on a NW-dipping back-thrust of the Northern Apennines chain. However, due to the uncertainties associated with its true structural interpretation, and the nearly similar depth at the hypocentral location with the Northern Apennines monocline, we associated the causative source of this earthquake to the interface between the upper plate and the Adria lithosphere of the lower plate, that represents the basal detachment level of the active outer thrust ramps of the Northern Apennines fold-and-thrust-belt.
A different seismotectonic interpretation of this event, can be drawn by the observation that the proposed source and the seismic sequence that occurred after the main shock, follow a NE-SW trend, that is transverse to the general structural grain of the thrust belt, and that is locally spatially coincident with one of the major transverse lineaments that crosses the Northern Apennines (i.e. the Prato-Sillaro Line, Auct.).
Although not well constrained, it appears that many of these transversal structures cutting across the mountain belt, are probably rooted in the subducting foreland plate, generated by changes of the dip of the monocline related to the inhomogeneous thickness of the Adriatic lithosphere related to the different paleogeographic domains involved in the subduction. Vannoli et al. (2015) proposed that these structures can be reactivate in the present-day stress regime, and are characterized by strike-slip or transpressional kinematics, as highlighted by many seismic sequences, and that some historical earthquakes may be associated to their activity, including the the Prato-Sillaro Line.
The issue of the seismogenic potential and the seismotectonics role of the transversal structures is object of debate, but we tentatively speculate that an alternative interpretation of the 2003 earthquake may be that it occurred on a secondary structure associated with the Prato-Sillaro Line, a tear fault dislocating the subducting slab (Nirta et al., 2007; Piccinini et al., 2014; Piana Agostinetti, 2015; Rosenbaum and Piana Agostinetti, 2015).
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS: What is the seismic potential of the transverse structure? Do they host only small magnitude sequences? Do they act only as segment boundaries for the larger thrust ramps?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Piccinini et al. (2006)
The authors present the seismological data recorded during the deployment of a local seismic network, installed after the 14 September 2003, Mw 5.3 Monghidoro earthquake. They recalculate the mainshock focal solution using polarities distribution, and make an accurate relative location of the aftershocks.
They also calculate the focal solutions of a subset of 148 aftershocks, in order to make a stress tensor inversion. According to the workers, the main shock occurred on a NW-dipping thrust at 20 km of depth, and under a NW-trending horizontal compression. They infer the direction of dip of the fault from cross-sections showing the distribution of the hypocenters of the aftershocks (confined between 15 and 22 km of depth).
